newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - BALANCING S.AFRICA'S BOP - BY E.OSBORN.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - BALANCING S.AFRICA'S BOP - BY E.OSBORN.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

After years of niggling the Reserve Bank has at last been persuaded that what to it was the most precise and accurate item in the Balance of Payments, namely net gold exports, has been progressively understating the correct position.

There was a time when its definition of the item as the bank's net foreign sales plus changes in the gold holdings of the banking sector was comprehensively correct in that the Bank was the sole exporter of gold. But in more recent years with the advent of the right of forward selling by the mining houses there have veen direct movements of gold in small bar form in settlement of forward sale contracts.
While the Economics and Statistics division of the Bank was sticking rigidly to its definition there was an increasing understatement of gold exports and hence credits to the balance of payments.

The Bank at last saw the light about October last year and introduced a series of revisions in the December Quarterly Bulletin to the gold exports retrospectively to 1992. The sum total of upward adjustments from 1992 to 1995 amounted to 4.7 billion rand. There was a corresponding improvement in balance of payments current account balances. The adjustment to the 1995 figures was particularly large at 2.4 billion and assisted in reducing the account deficit to 12.7 billion as shown in the September Bulletin to one of 10.2 billion in the December Bulletin.

The Reserve Bank supplies the monthly gold export figures to the Commissioner of Customs and Excise for incorporation in the monthly trade data, without question or challenge. So it was with the Bank waking up to its mistakes that it supplied a largish correction to the gold figures for the earlier months of 1996 and which accounted for a phenomenal apparent increase in the trade balance from 0.7 billion in September to 3.9 billion in October. The current month's trade is, of course, derived as the difference between the accumulated trade data of successive months.

The Commissioner publishes the preliminary trade data on a cumulative basis which takes in the trade of the current month as well as corrections to past months. The practice is unfortunate in that the derived current month's figures are distorted by the corrections of the past months. Monthly trade patterns are never correct, thus providing an unsound basis for attempting to adjust the figures in respect of currency depreciation. This is particularly important when there is a rapid rate of depreciation as was the case in 1996. In the crudest terms, for example, nominal exports grew by 23.5 percent in 1996 but in real terms by 4.3 percent. Similarly, the nominal growth of imports was 18.8 percent but only 2.0 percent in currency adjusted terms.

The Reserve Bank has just announced that it intends revising the net gold exports for the second and third quarters of 1996 in the forthcoming March Quarterly Bulletin. It had revised the first quarter upwards by 536 million in the December Bulletin. It rather lamely explained that more comprehensive data has now become available. The time delay is incomprehensible give the fact that information for the gold mining industry is extremely comprehensive and exact, and that there are really only two sources of outward movements of gold, namely the Reserve Bank itself and the Rand Refinery at Germiston, other than illicit gold trade. The average rand realisations on gold sales, both spot and forward, are revealed in the quarterly gold mining results of the industry within two to three weeks of the end of the quarter.

However, the upshot of this announcement is the current account deficit for 1996 is more likely to be closer to the 10 billion mark than the 12 billion plus, which the December Bulletin figures for the first three quarters of 1996 was indicating. The accumulated deficit for the first three quarters amounted to 10.5 billion in that release. It is also to be hoped that the Reserve Bank will correct the definition of net gold sales as shown in the footnotes of the balance of payments table at the same time.

But there are further revisions to the 1995 balance of payments estimates that are necessitated by the latest Commisioner's trade release for the twelve months of 1996, which also shows the revised figures for 1995. The nature of the revisions indicates that they are in respect of South Africa's trade and not other members of the Customs Union, bearing in mind that the trade data refer to the Customs Union as a whole.

For exports there are significant adjustments in respect of foodstuffs (+502 million rand), mineral products (+490 million), precious minerals (+215 million), paper products (-212 million) and a net additional 57 million for the machinery and vehicles categories. Altogether exports are increased by 1,039 million and this is apart from any gold adjustments.
On the import side machinery is reduced by 743 million rand and the total downward adjustment to imports is 834 million, giving a total net improvement to the trade balance of 1,873 million.

Now the Reserve Bank had shown a partial adjustment to the 1995 non-gold merchandise trade estimates in the balance of payments between its September and December issues amounting to 779 million in net terms. Accordingly a further correction of 1.1 billion is required for the 1995 estimates, thus reducing the current account deficit to 9.1 billion.
There will have to be a compensating correction to the balancing item in the capital account, which is euphemistically described as "non-monetary private sector" short-term capital movements.

The full year balance of payments estimates for 1995 were first published in the March 1996 Quarterly Bulletin. The current account deficit was then shown as 12.7 billion. As demonstrated above it should be finalised as 9.1 billion. Capital account movements should be reduced by a corresponding 3.6 billion.
No doubt one can moralise on faulty policy decisions being made on the basis of incorrect statistics.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
